newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, new securites absorbed.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, new securites absorbed.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries erased early strength and ended lower on Wednesday, even as the stock market rejoiced at the two-party control of the government that remained intact after Tuesday's U.S. election.

While the stock market rallied to new highs, the U.S. Treasury market, which rallied on Tuesday in anticipation of the election result, busied itself with absorbing the $10.0 billion in new 10-year notes auctioned by the Treasury in the second leg of its three-part quarterly refunding.

After the afternoon deadline for 10-year note bids passed and the auction results were announced, the market's losses widened as players positioned themselves ahead of the 30-year Treasury bond auction on Thursday, analysts said.

The downward drift was "profit-taking, book-squaring, consolidation after recent gains, and getting ready for the 30-year bond auction," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond ended at 101-22/32 on Wednesday, down 14/32 to 6.62 percent, retracing almost half the advance it scored on Tuesday.
The Treasury's new 10-year notes were sold at an average 6.273 percent yield, in line with expectations, analysts said.
"The auction went well, all things considered," said Flanagan. "The market rallied going into the auction and you could have made a case that it was over-priced."
Flanagan said the 2.41 bid-to-cover ratio, the value of bids received over the value of bids accepted, was in line with the long run average for 10-year auctions.
"Today's (10-year) auction was fine," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at CS First Boston. "I'd give it a 'B' -- not bad but not great either."

Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. said the market's afternoon losses were more the function of players wanting to let the market cheapen up a little before the 30-year Treasury bond auction on Thursday than a negative reaction to Wednesday's 10-year auction results.
"The market is setting up for the 30-year," said Moran, referring to the sale of $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds the Treasury has set for Thursday.
Moran observed that in contrast to stocks' post-election rally, Treasuries rallied on Monday and Tuesday "in anticipation of the 'split government' election outcome."

The financial markets have applauded the results of the U.S. election because investors believe a Republican Congress will reinforce the Democratic President's commitment to fiscal conservatism and a balanced federal budget.
For prices to go higher from current levels, the market needs to see more weak economic data, analysts said.
"I don't think we'll see 6.50 (percent) on the bond yield unless we get more weak economic or low inflation numbers," said Moran.
The market doesn't get such influential data until next week. The October Producer Price report is due Wednesday.
The October Consumer Price Index (CPI) and retail sales data are due on Thursday, November 14.
At the close of trade on Wednesday, three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.02 percent and 5.07 percent, respectively. One-year bill rates rose one basis point to 5.14 percent.
Two-year notes slipped 3/32 to 100-7/32 to yield 5.76 pct. Five-year notes fell 4/32 to 100-27/32 to yield 6.05 percent.
Ten-year notes dropped 6/32 to 101-16/32, erasing a third of Tuesday's gain, to yield 6.29 percent.
--North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
